newsitem.title: USA: U.S. heating oil retail prices said to have peaked.
newsitem.headline: U.S. heating oil retail prices said to have peaked.

text.p: After fears of a home heating oil shortage sent prices skyrocketing last month, heating oil retailers say prices have peaked now that refiners have proven they can meet demand.

"My guess is, even if there is some colder-than-normal weather, it seems to be that prices have peaked for the winter," said Robert Greenes, spokesman for New York Oil Heating Association Inc, a heating oil retailers trade group.
Refiners have increased heating oil inventories by almost six million barrels in the last three weeks in the U.S. Northeast, the largest heating oil market in the world.
Production of distillates, which include heating oil, have hovered around record levels in the last month.
This eased concerns refiners would not be able to replenish stocks fast enough ahead of wintery cold snaps.

"It's a fair assessment that dealers have filled their tanks to a point where we have reached a level of security that we haven't had in the past year," said Jack Sullivan, head of the New England Fuel Institute, a Massachusetts group which represents 1,400 heating oil retailers and wholesalers.
Alfred Allegretti, president of Bayside Fuel Oil Depot Corp, a major retailer and wholesaler of heating oil based in Brooklyn, New York, said a shortage was never a real threat.
"It was a just big scare," said Allegretti, adding: "Refiners have proven themselves extremely flexible, and we have plenty of supplies now."

Economists and dealers said the spike in heating oil prices assumed the possibility of shortage during the winter, enabling heating oil to fetch retail prices in November normally not seen until the thick of winter in January.

"I think the high price is already in the market. Given an average winter, I think prices would have a difficult time advancing since we got the seasonal price rise early," said John Paul Murphy, senior economist at the Massachusetts state energy office.
Murphy said the average price for a gallon of heating oil in Massachusetts is now $1.12, almost 20 cents more than a year ago.

The high price reflects what retailers had to pay for heating oil futures last month on New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) when heating oil for November delivery hit a post-Gulf War high of 76.75 cents a gallon.

Cheryl Trench, an economist with Petroleum Industry Research Foundation, doubts heating oil futures on NYMEX will hit that level again this winter, barring a prolonged spell of unusually cold weather. "The notion that prices have topped is probably correct, though we may get another spike if there is a cold snap."

But Trench also warned prices could shot up fast due to a supply disruption at any one of a number of refiners which now favor producing at a feverish pace to tailor stocks to current demand rather than maintaining high stocks to meet that demand.
Because this "just-in-time" output program is relatively new to the oil industry, uncertainty remains as to whether refiners would be able to produce enough in a real pinch.
The situation was particulary dire in October since heating oil inventories had not built significantly from historical lows since the spring.

Refiners had traditionally begun socking away heating oil inventories during the summer in preparation for winter, but because of the just-in-time strategy, production schedules have been adjusted to more closely reflect current demand.
Inventories therefore remain lean under the strategy and vulnerable to longer periods of high demand, analysts said.
However, given the the sudden replenishment in heating oil stocks in recent weeks, dealers are showing signs of relief.

"A big concern is a cold snap, but our refinery industry has shown it is pretty resilient," said Michael Ferrante, president of the Massachusetts Oilheat Council Inc, another heating oil retailer trade group.
--New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1620
